newsitem.title: INDIA: Pakistan optimistic ahead of new talks with India.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan optimistic ahead of new talks with India.

text.p: On the eve of a fresh round of discussions, Pakistan said it expected progress in peace talks with India no matter who ruled in New Delhi.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan played down the impact of India's current political crisis, saying he hoped peace talks would move forward even if Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda failed to survive a confidence vote on Friday.
"By and large the foreign policy of India may not undergo a drastic change," Khan told Cable News Network (CNN) television in an interview.
"We are hopeful whichever government there is, existing or a new government, that we'd continue this dialogue in a fruitful manner."
Khan, in New Delhi for a meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement, is scheduled to talk with Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral over breakfast at 9 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Wednesday.
The talks follow four days of discussions last month between the two nations' foreign secretaries -- the highest civil servants in the foreign ministries.

The foreign secretaries ended their talks on March 31 on an upbeat note and agreed to meet again in Islamabad. But they did not set a date, partly because of the political turmoil in Delhi which threatens the survival of Deve Gowda's government.
Diplomats said the talks on Wednesday were not expected to last long, and Khan was scheduled to leave New Delhi on the same day.
But Indian and Pakistani officials held out the prospect of a subsequent round of foreign secretary-level talks after Friday's parliamentary vote.
They said whoever was Indian prime minister in May could be expected to meet his Pakistani counterpart Nawaz Sharif on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Maldives.

During his three days in the Indian capital, Khan has sounded optimistic about progress in the talks, which were in limbo for more than three years until last month as the two nations traded accusations over disputed Kashmir.
On Sunday, Khan said there was no reason the two longtime rivals could not improve strained ties.

"If the relations between Japan and America could improve after the Second World War, or relations between Germany and Britain, or Germany and France, or the Russians and the western European countries could improve, when the Berlin Wall could come down, why is India sticking on to a small point?" he said.
"Pakistan today is in a position to talk on substantial issues," he told CNN. "We should talk and talk, and that's what we'll do. We'll talk, we will not allow the talks to break."
Pakistan considers Kashmir, divided since 1947 between the neighbouring countries, the core issue in talks and in the past has linked progress in other areas such as trade to Kashmir.
India is willing to settle other, less contentious matters first.
But The Times of India on Tuesday quoted Khan as saying his government believed in a step-by-step approach, and urged India to reduce the number of security forces in Kashmir as a first step.
Khan said that if the two countries settled their problems, they would unleash great dynamism. "We could both of us be super tigers in Asia," he said.
